title: Locks on hearts
hookLine: do they not reflect on the Qur'an, or are there locks on their hearts (47:24)

cards: You can read a page and arrive at the bottom with no idea what was on it. Eyes moved. Mind was elsewhere.
It happens with a contract, a textbook, an email from a boss. People do it with scripture too, sometimes beautifully: a flawless recitation, every vowel in place, and nothing reaching the heart.
Surah Muhammad has a question about that, and a picture you can almost hear: a lock, clicking shut.

teach.h: TADABBUR: FOLLOW A VERSE PAST ITS END.
teach.b: Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's translation: "Will they then not meditate on the Qur'an, or are there locks on the hearts?" The Arabic verb behind meditate is yatadabbarun; its noun is tadabbur.

teach.h: D-B-R: THE BACK, WHAT COMES AFTER.
teach.b: The root d-b-r means the back of something, what comes after. Lexicons explain tadabbur as looking at the end of a matter, thinking through where a thing leads. So it isn't just reading.
It's following a verse past its last word: what does this ask of me, where does it lead, what changes if I mean it. The Qur'an asks for this more than once.

Surah An-Nisa' asks the same question, will they not ponder the Qur'an. Surah Sad says the book was sent down, blessed, so that people would ponder its verses and those with understanding would take heed. Then the lock.

teach.h: EACH HEART WITH ITS OWN LOCK.
teach.b: The verse says locks, plural, on hearts, plural, and the Arabic adds a small word, aqfaluha, their locks, as if each heart has its own lock fitted to it.
Commentators read it as a heart sealed by habit, pride or carelessness until nothing gets in.
Some scholars treat the question as a mirror for believers, especially the ones who read often, not an accusation thrown at outsiders.
A report in Sunan an-Nasa'i, from Abu Dharr, says the Prophet ﷺ once stood in prayer through a night repeating a single verse until morning. The point wasn't how far he got. It was how deep.

how: Alongside recitation, some Muslims join tadabbur circles or read a few verses daily with a tafsir, pausing to ask what each verse asks of them; some repeat a single verse many times in night prayer.

o: memorizing a surah by repeating it many times
reciting a verse with every vowel perfectly in place
pondering a verse until you see where it leads

games.q: locks on hearts — tap the pairs.
p: their locks, one for each heart
sent down so people would ponder

s: it means pondering where a verse leads, past its last word.
the Qur'an asks people to ponder it in more than one surah
An-Nisa' and Sad ask it too.
some scholars read the verse as a mirror for believers
it is not only aimed at outsiders; it warns regular readers too.

games.q: you have a free evening and the Qur'an open. by Abu Dharr's report, what did the Prophet once do through a night?
o: repeated a single verse until morning.
games.why: Abu Dharr reports he repeated one verse until morning; depth, not distance.

practice: Take today's verse, will they not meditate, or are there locks on the hearts, and say it slowly in your head. Then ask the three questions of tadabbur: what does it say, what does it ask of me, where does it lead if I mean it?
Stay with whichever question opens something, and if you pray, you can ask for the lock to open.

wordCard.voice: Tadabbur. Pondering that follows a verse past its last word, from the root for what comes after, asked for in 47:24. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: pondering, reflecting on where something leads.

carryVoice: Your line: unlock the heart. Every heart, the verse suggests, has a lock of its own. See you tomorrow.
